passage:
Jahnavi caught up with Jomon outside the science lab. "Jo, can I take your notes again? Just for chapter six."
"Sure," said Jomon. He handed over the notebook. Jahnavi grinned and disappeared.
"That's the fourth time this week," said Kunal, who was leaning on the wall.
"It's fine."
"Is it? You didn't even finish your own homework yesterday. You were on the phone with Meena for two hours."
Jomon shrugged. "She was crying."
"And the day before, you did that poster for Aman."
"Someone had to."
"Do you want to?" Kunal asked.
Jomon looked at his empty hands. "I don't know. I just... don't know how to say no. Everyone thinks I like it."
Kunal said nothing. Then, "Maybe start with one thing?"

qa.q: What did Jahnavi ask Jomon for outside the science lab?
qa.a: Jahnavi asked to take Jomon's notes again, just for chapter six.

qa.q: What is Jomon feeling as he looks at his empty hands and says he doesn't know how to say no?
qa.a: Jomon feels drained, stuck and quietly resentful. People assume he enjoys helping, so he cannot easily step out of the role.

qa.q: What small first step could Jomon try, as Kunal hints?
qa.a: Jomon could pick one request, such as the notes, and say he needs his own time this evening, offering a later day instead.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see Jomon's usual yes?
qa.a: Jahnavi probably takes it as easy willingness, since Jomon hands over the notes with no complaint. Jahnavi may not know it costs him anything.

grounding: A teenager everyone turns to for favours feels drained and quietly resentful, and finds it hard to step out of the reliable role.

passage:
I'm Aparna. Nobody planned it, but I became the person people find in the corridor. Maria wants my maths notes. Someone else needs a lift with a chart. A friend has cried on my shoulder three times this month, and at some point I stopped asking myself whether I had the energy.
Last Thursday I sat on the bus with my bag heavy and my chest tight. My phone buzzed with another message from Maria: "Can you send me tomorrow's worksheet too? You're a lifesaver."
I felt something sour when I read that. It wasn't Maria's fault. I had never once said no.
So I typed, "I can't tonight. I'll send it tomorrow morning." She replied, "Oh okay." My hands were shaking as if I had done something huge. I'm not sure yet how to stop being the reliable one, but that was a start.

qa.q: What did Maria ask Aparna to send?
qa.a: Maria asked for tomorrow's worksheet.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling when reading Maria's message, and why?
qa.a: Aparna felt something sour, like resentment and tiredness. The bag felt heavy and the chest tight, and Aparna had never said no.

qa.q: What did Aparna try that started to change the pattern?
qa.a: Aparna replied that the worksheet would come tomorrow morning and not tonight. It was a small no with a kind alternative.

qa.q: How might Maria have felt on receiving the reply that the worksheet would come tomorrow?
qa.a: Maria was probably a little surprised, since the reply was just "Oh okay." Maria may not have realised how much Aparna had been carrying.

grounding: A teenager everyone turns to for notes and comfort grows drained and resentful, and finds the reliable role hard to leave.

passage: At the temple fair in Hosur, Saurabh couldn't walk ten steps without someone calling him. "Saurabh, my phone screen froze!" "Saurabh, take this box to the stall!" "Saurabh, my brother failed maths again, can you teach him on Sunday?" He said yes each time, the easy smile on his face. It had been like this since he fixed the panchayat office printer in Class 9. At sixteen, the whole lane thought of him as the boy who never says no. Tonight he helped carry lanterns until his arms ached. His friend Mohit found him sitting behind the balloon stall, staring at nothing. "You okay?" "I'm fine," Saurabh said, then heard how flat it sounded. Mohit tugged a plate of jalebi toward him. "Eat. I'll tell people you've gone home." Saurabh didn't argue.

qa.q: Where was the temple fair?
qa.a: In Hosur.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling behind the balloon stall?
qa.a: He felt drained and a little numb, his 'I'm fine' sounding flat even to himself after a night of saying yes.

qa.q: How could Mohit support Saurabh beyond tonight?
qa.a: He could help Saurabh practise saying 'not today' to one request, and step in with the lane sometimes so Saurabh isn't always the one called.

qa.q: How does the lane see Saurabh?
qa.a: They see him as the boy who never says no, a reliable helper, without noticing how tired he is.

grounding: Shows a teenager who has become the reliable helper for everyone, now drained and stuck in that role.

passage: In the school corridor in Johannesburg, Rafael caught up with Zanele just before the bell. "Hey, can you do my slides for the history project? My gran's visiting, I've got no time." Zanele heard herself say, "Sure." It was the fourth favour this week. She had already lent her calculator, walked the new girl to the sick bay, and spent Tuesday lunch listening to her friend Lindiwe cry about a boy. That night she made Rafael's slides and did her own, finishing after midnight. At breakfast she snapped at her little brother for singing. On the bus she scrolled through the group chat. Fourteen messages, three with her name in them. She put the phone face-down on her knee and closed her eyes. "Why am I always the one?" she thought, and then felt guilty for thinking it.

qa.q: What did Rafael ask Zanele to do?
qa.a: He asked her to do his slides for the history project.

qa.q: How did Zanele feel on the bus?
qa.a: She felt drained and quietly resentful, wondering why she was always the one, and then guilty for thinking it.

qa.q: What would you advise Zanele before the next favour?
qa.a: Pause before answering, and try one small honest reply like, 'I can't this week, sorry,' to start stepping out of the always-yes role.

qa.q: How might Zanele's little brother experience her morning?
qa.a: He was just singing and got snapped at, so he may feel confused or hurt without knowing why.

grounding: Shows a teenager everyone depends on for favours becoming drained and resentful and finding it hard to stop saying yes.

passage: By nine at night there was a queue outside Keerthana's door in the girls' hostel, even if nobody called it that. Pooja needed her chemistry notes photographed. Her roommate wanted to cry about a fight with her mother, again. Then a message from Mohit in the class group: "Keerthana you have the physics answers na? Send pls 🙏" She sent them. She always did. Afterwards she sat on her bed with her own homework untouched and noticed that her jaw was tight. When Pooja knocked again, "Just one tiny thing," Keerthana heard herself say "Sure!" in her brightest voice, then shut the door and stared at the wall. Nobody had asked how her day was. She realised nobody ever did, and that she had never given them a reason to.

qa.q: What did Mohit ask for in the class group?
qa.a: He asked for the physics answers.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling as she sat with her own homework untouched?
qa.a: She felt drained and quietly resentful; her jaw was tight even though she kept saying yes.

qa.q: What small step could Keerthana try tomorrow?
qa.a: She could tell Pooja, "Not tonight, I need to do my own work," and share notes at one set time instead of whenever someone asks.

qa.q: How might Pooja see Keerthana?
qa.a: Pooja probably sees her as the cheerful one who never minds, because the bright "Sure!" hides how tired she is.

grounding: Shows a teenager whom everyone relies on for notes, comfort and favours starting to feel drained and resentful in that role.
